propositions.text: The appeal concerns injuries to a prisoner and a prison guard during transportation between Montréal courthouse and Laval penitentiary.
propositions.quote: This appeal concerns a prisoner and a prison guard who both suffered injuries during the transportation of the prisoner by the prison guard between the court house in Montréal and a penitentiary in nearby Laval.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the appeal concerns injuries to a prisoner and prison guard during transportation between Montréal courthouse and Laval penitentiary.

propositions.text: The prisoner was charged with assault causing bodily harm, assault of a peace officer, and intimidation of a justice system participant.
propositions.quote: The prisoner was charged as a result with assault causing bodily harm, assault of a peace officer and intimidation of a justice system participant.

propositions.text: The appellant is Riccardo Bellusci and the alleged victim in all three cases is prison guard Michel Asselin.
propositions.quote: The appellant, Riccardo Bellusci, was the prisoner. And the alleged victim, in all three cases, was the prison guard, Michel Asselin.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the prisoner was charged with assault and intimidation; appellant is Bellusci and victim is guard Asselin.

propositions.text: Bellusci was acquitted at trial of both assault charges, and these acquittals are not in issue before the Court.
propositions.quote: Mr. Bellusci was acquitted at trial of both charges of assault, and his acquittals are not in issue before us.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Bellusci was acquitted of assault charges, and these acquittals are not before the Court.

propositions.text: The appeal relates solely to the intimidation charge, for which the trial judge found Bellusci guilty.
propositions.quote: This appeal relates solely to the charge of intimidation. The trial judge found that Mr. Bellusci’s guilt on that count had been established by the Crown.

propositions.text: The trial judge declined to enter a conviction due to a violation of Bellusci’s s. 7 Charter rights.
propositions.quote: He nonetheless declined to enter a conviction on the ground that Mr. Bellusci’s rights under s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms had been violated (2008 QCCQ 21567 (CanLII)).

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the appeal concerns intimidation charge; trial judge found guilt but declined conviction due to s.7 Charter violation.

propositions.text: Bellusci was charged with uttering threats to a prison guard who recklessly provoked him and then assaulted him while restrained and in custody.
propositions.quote: Mr. Bellusci stood charged with uttering threats to a prison guard who had recklessly provoked him and then, in response to the threats, grievously assaulted him while he was chained, shackled, handcuffed and defenceless — in the prison guard’s custody.

propositions.text: Bellusci was entitled under s. 24(1) of the Charter to a constitutional remedy for this egregious breach of rights.
propositions.quote: For this egregious breach of his constitutional rights, Mr. Bellusci was entitled under s. 24(1) of the Charter to a constitutional remedy.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Bellusci was charged with threats after reckless provocation and assault while restrained; he was entitled to a Charter remedy.

propositions.text: Section 24(1) of the Charter gives trial judges broad discretion to grant an appropriate and just remedy.
propositions.quote: Section 24(1) of the Charter vests in trial judges broad discretion in granting, according to its terms, “such remedy as the court considers appropriate and just in the circumstances”.

propositions.text: The trial judge considered lesser alternatives and concluded only a stay of proceedings was appropriate and just in this case.
propositions.quote: After considering lesser alternatives, the trial judge concluded that nothing short of a stay of proceedings would be an appropriate and just remedy in the exceptional circumstances of this case.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states s.24(1) grants broad discretion; trial judge found only a stay of proceedings appropriate and just here.

propositions.text: The trial judge made no error of law or reviewable error of fact in exercising his discretion.
propositions.quote: In exercising his discretion as he did, the trial judge committed no error of law, nor any reviewable error of fact.

propositions.text: The trial judge’s conclusion was not manifestly unjust under governing authorities.
propositions.quote: His conclusion was not manifestly unjust, within the meaning of the governing authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the trial judge made no legal or factual error and his conclusion was not manifestly unjust.

propositions.text: The Quebec Court of Appeal quashed the stay and remitted the matter to trial court for continuation on Crown appeal.
propositions.quote: On an appeal by the Crown, the Quebec Court of Appeal nonetheless quashed the stay and remitted the matter to the trial court for continuation of Mr. Bellusci’s trial (2010 QCCA 2118 (CanLII)).

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal erred in setting aside the stay of proceedings entered at trial.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I believe the Court of Appeal erred in setting aside the stay of proceedings entered at trial.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the Court of Appeal quashed the stay and erred in doing so.

propositions.text: This error alone suffices to allow Bellusci’s appeal and restore the stay of proceedings.
propositions.quote: This alone is sufficient to allow Mr. Bellusci’s appeal to this Court against the judgment of the Court of Appeal, and to restore the stay of proceedings entered by the trial judge.

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes the error suffices to allow Bellusci’s appeal and restore the stay of proceedings.

propositions.text: Whether the Court of Appeal was entitled to order continuation of proceedings or was bound to order a new trial after setting aside the stay.
propositions.quote: Was the Court of Appeal entitled, upon setting aside the stay, to order continuation of the proceedings before the trial court, or was it bound instead to order a new trial?

paragraphs.summary: The Court raises the issue whether the Court of Appeal could order continuation or must order a new trial after setting aside the stay.

propositions.text: The issue is important, unresolved by the Court, and was thoroughly canvassed by parties and interveners.
propositions.quote: This is an important issue, not previously resolved by the Court. It was thoroughly canvassed by both parties, by the amicus curiae, and by the intervener as well.

propositions.text: The Court will provide guidance on this issue for appellate courts facing it as an actual matter.
propositions.quote: In these circumstances, I think it appropriate to provide guidance on the issue for the benefit of appellate courts before which it is bound to arise as an actual ― and not theoretical ― matter.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the issue is important and unresolved; it will provide guidance for appellate courts.

propositions.text: On May 15, 2007, Bellusci was a prisoner transported in a van driven by Asselin.
propositions.quote: On May 15, 2007, Mr. Bellusci was a prisoner being transported in a van driven by Mr. Asselin.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Bellusci was transported in a van driven by Asselin on May 15, 2007.

propositions.text: The Crown alleged Bellusci assaulted Asselin without provocation and threatened to rape his wife and children.
propositions.quote: The Crown alleged that Mr. Bellusci, on that occasion, assaulted Mr. Asselin without provocation and threatened to rape his wife and children.

propositions.text: Bellusci admitted the threats but contended Asselin assaulted him.
propositions.quote: Mr. Bellusci admitted the threats but contended that Mr. Asselin had in fact assaulted him.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown alleged Bellusci assaulted and threatened Asselin; Bellusci admitted threats but claimed Asselin assaulted him.

propositions.text: The trial judge had reasonable doubt Bellusci assaulted Asselin but was satisfied Bellusci threatened to sexually assault Asselin’s wife and children.
propositions.quote: The trial judge was left with a reasonable doubt whether Mr. Bellusci had assaulted Mr. Asselin, but he was satisfied that Mr. Bellusci had threatened to sexually assault Mr. Asselin’s wife and children.

propositions.text: The judge acquitted Bellusci of assault but found him guilty of intimidating Asselin, a justice system participant.
propositions.quote: The judge therefore acquitted Mr. Bellusci of the assault charges, but found that Mr. Bellusci was guilty of intimidating Mr. Asselin, a justice system participant.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge doubted assault but found Bellusci guilty of intimidation for threats to Asselin’s family.

propositions.text: The trial judge found on balance of probabilities: (a) Bellusci verbally abused Asselin; (b) Asselin endangered Bellusci by disclosing he was a rapist; (c) Bellusci threatened to rape Asselin’s family in response; (d) Asselin was injured when Bellusci forced open the cell door; (e) Asselin then assaulted Bellusci while he was restrained.
propositions.quote: (a) Mr. Bellusci had subjected Mr. Asselin [translation] “to verbal attacks that were abusive, insulting and crude” (para. 26); (b) Mr. Asselin had placed Mr. Bellusci in danger by disclosing to the other prisoners in the van that Mr. Bellusci was a rapist; (c) Mr. Bellusci then, in response, threatened to rape Mr. Asselin’s wife and children; (d) Mr. Asselin was injured when, as he was opening the cell door, Mr. Bellusci forced it upon him; and (e) Mr. Asselin then assaulted and injured Mr. Bellusci, who was at the time, chained, handcuffed and shackled in a secure cell in the prison van.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found Bellusci abused Asselin verbally, Asselin endangered Bellusci, Bellusci threatened family, Asselin injured opening door, then assaulted restrained Bellusci.

propositions.text: The trial judge held Bellusci’s s.7 Charter rights were violated based on these undisputed findings.
propositions.quote: On the basis of these findings ― which are not in dispute ― the trial judge held that Mr. Bellusci’s constitutional rights under s. 7 of the Charter had been violated.

propositions.text: It would shock the public to convict Bellusci for threats recklessly provoked and unlawfully punished by the guard.
propositions.quote: It would shock informed members of the public to enter a conviction against Mr. Bellusci for having uttered verbal threats recklessly provoked and unlawfully punished by the prison guard to whom the threats had been made.

propositions.text: After considering other remedies, the trial judge held a stay of proceedings was the only appropriate remedy in this unusual case.
propositions.quote: After considering other available remedies, including a reduction of sentence and the possibility of legal or disciplinary proceedings against Mr. Asselin, the trial judge held that a stay of proceedings was the only appropriate remedy in the unusual and troubling circumstances of this case.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found Bellusci’s s.7 rights violated and only a stay of proceedings was appropriate remedy after considering others.

propositions.text: A trial judge’s s.24(1) Charter remedy order should be disturbed on appeal only if misdirected or clearly wrong causing injustice.
propositions.quote: It is well established that a trial judge’s order under s. 24(1) of the Charter should be disturbed on appeal “only if the trial judge misdirects himself or if his decision is so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice”: R. v. Regan, 2002 SCC 12, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 297, at para. 117; Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Tobiass, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 391, at para. 87.

paragraphs.summary: The Court cites authority that a trial judge’s s.24(1) remedy should be disturbed only if misdirected or clearly wrong causing injustice.

propositions.text: The Court unanimously reaffirmed the standard of review for s.24(1) remedies in R. v. Bjelland.
propositions.quote: That this is the appropriate standard of review was unanimously reaffirmed by the Court, citing Regan, in R. v. Bjelland, 2009 SCC 38, [2009] 2 S.C.R. 651 (Rothstein J., at para. 15; Fish J., at para. 51).

propositions.text: Once infringement established, trial judge must grant appropriate remedy vindicating rights, fair to parties, considering all circumstances.
propositions.quote: On an application under s. 24(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms , once an infringement has been established, the trial judge must grant “such remedy as [is] appropriate and just in the circumstances”. The remedy granted must vindicate the rights of the claimant, be fair to the party against whom it is ordered, and consider all other relevant circumstances.

propositions.text: Appellate courts may interfere only if trial judge erred in law or rendered unjust decision, especially given wide discretion under s.24(1).
propositions.quote: Appellate courts may interfere with a trial judge’s exercise of discretion only if the trial judge has erred in law or rendered an unjust decision. This is particularly true of remedies granted by trial judges under s. 24(1) of the Charter , which by its very terms confers on trial judges the widest possible discretion.

propositions.text: Appellate courts must not substitute their discretion for trial judge’s merely because they would have granted a different remedy.
propositions.quote: Finally, appellate courts must take particular care not to substitute their own exercise of discretion for that of the trial judge merely because they would have granted a more generous or more limited remedy.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains the standard of review for s.24(1) remedies and appellate restraint in interfering with trial judge discretion.

propositions.text: The appeal outcome depends on whether the trial judge misdirected, erred in fact, or rendered an unjust decision.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the outcome of this appeal depends on whether the trial judge misdirected himself in law, committed a reviewable error of fact or rendered a decision that is “so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice”.

propositions.text: The trial judge’s decision suffers from none of these fatal flaws.
propositions.quote: In my view, his decision suffers from none of these fatal flaws.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the appeal depends on errors by trial judge, but finds none of these flaws present.

propositions.text: The trial judge clearly and correctly outlined applicable law and jurisprudence and considered appropriate factors with evidence.
propositions.quote: The trial judge first clearly and correctly outlined the applicable principles of law and relevant jurisprudence. He then considered the appropriate factors in light of the evidence before him.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the trial judge correctly outlined law and considered factors with evidence.

propositions.text: The Charter breach was in the residual and exceptional category of egregious misconduct offensive to proceed with the case.
propositions.quote: he felt the Charter breach in issue here fell within the “residual” and “exceptional” category of cases where the misconduct was “so egregious that the mere fact of going forward in the light of it will be offensive” (Tobiass, at para. 91).

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the Charter breach was egregious and residual, making proceeding offensive.

propositions.text: The trial judge held the case involved unlawful extrajudicial punishment shocking to the public.
propositions.quote: The trial judge held that this was a case of unlawful extrajudicial punishment that would shock the public.

propositions.text: Mr. Bellusci was attacked by a state agent while restrained in a secure prison van.
propositions.quote: Mr. Bellusci was attacked by an agent of the state while chained, handcuffed, shackled and confined to his cell in a secure prison van.

propositions.text: The attack was an apparent act of revenge by a prison guard to physically punish Mr. Bellusci.
propositions.quote: This was an apparent act of revenge by a prison guard who decided to make Mr. Bellusci “pay physically” for his unacceptable conduct (para. 21).

propositions.text: Mr. Bellusci suffered significant injuries including wire mesh imprints, forearm deformation, and head and neck bumps.
propositions.quote: The injuries inflicted on Mr. Bellusci were hardly trivial. They included “imprints of wire mesh with petechiae on the back of the left shoulder at the level of the shoulder blade, . . . injuries causing deformation of the left forearm, [and] bumps and injuries on the head and neck” (para. 34).

propositions.text: Due to head injury, Mr. Bellusci was observed overnight in the prison infirmary.
propositions.quote: As a result of his head injury, Mr. Bellusci was kept under observation overnight in the prison infirmary.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found Mr. Bellusci was unlawfully punished by a prison guard while restrained, suffering serious injuries and requiring medical observation.

propositions.text: The trial judge found Mr. Bellusci’s threats likely resulted from Mr. Asselin’s inappropriate disclosure of his sexual offender status.
propositions.quote: The trial judge was satisfied that the appellant’s threats, however reprehensible, would in all likelihood not have been uttered but for Mr. Asselin’s inappropriate disclosure to the other prisoners that the appellant was a sexual offender.

propositions.text: The trial judge acknowledged prison guards’ difficult position but found it did not justify Mr. Asselin’s disclosure jeopardizing Mr. Bellusci’s safety.
propositions.quote: The trial judge was clearly alive to the difficult position of prison guards, but this could not justify Mr. Asselin’s disclosure, which jeopardized Mr. Bellusci’s personal safety while imprisoned.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found Mr. Asselin’s disclosure caused threats against Mr. Bellusci and was unjustified despite guards’ difficulties.

propositions.text: The trial judge found the justice system’s integrity was tarnished by reticence and solidarity among prison guards at trial.
propositions.quote: The integrity of the justice system was further tarnished, in the judge’s view, by the reticence and “sclerotic solidarity” that characterized the testimony at trial of Mr. Asselin’s fellow prison guards (para. 79).

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found prison guards’ reticence and solidarity tarnished justice system integrity.

propositions.text: The trial judge found it was open to decline conviction due to intolerable abuse by a state actor.
propositions.quote: Having found that Mr. Bellusci had been provoked and subjected by a state actor to intolerable physical and psychological abuse, it was open to the trial judge to decline to enter a conviction against him.

propositions.text: Tobiass explains serious past abuse can undermine public confidence and justify a stay of proceedings.
propositions.quote: As the Court explained in Tobiass, “if a past abuse were serious enough, then public confidence in the administration of justice could be so undermined that the mere act of carrying forward in the light of it would constitute a new and ongoing abuse sufficient to warrant a stay of proceedings” (para. 96).

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found declining conviction was open due to abuse; Tobiass supports stay if public confidence is undermined.

propositions.text: I cannot agree the trial judge erred by overlooking the non sequitur between misconduct and stay of proceedings.
propositions.quote: I am therefore unable to share the conclusion of the Court of Appeal that the trial judge, in granting a stay, committed a reviewable error by overlooking the “non sequitur” between the state misconduct and the stay of proceedings (para. 21).

paragraphs.summary: The Court disagrees with the Court of Appeal that the trial judge erred in granting a stay due to non sequitur.

propositions.text: I do not agree the trial judge erred by failing to consider less drastic remedies; he expressly considered and rejected them.
propositions.quote: Nor am I able to agree that the trial judge erred in failing to consider the availability of less drastic remedies. On the contrary, as mentioned earlier, he expressly considered various alternatives and found that none were adequate in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the trial judge properly considered and rejected less drastic remedies.

propositions.text: The trial judge concluded only a stay was sufficient and appropriate given the misconduct’s seriousness and impact.
propositions.quote: Given the seriousness and the impact of the prison guard’s misconduct, the trial judge concluded that only a stay would be sufficient and appropriate in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge concluded only a stay was adequate due to the misconduct’s seriousness and impact.

propositions.text: The trial judge balanced competing interests including guards’ position, justice system integrity, charges’ seriousness, and rights violation gravity before granting stay.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the trial judge appreciated the need to balance the competing interests at play in contemplating a stay of proceedings. He expressly took into account the difficult position of prison guards, the importance to the justice system of ensuring their protection, the seriousness of the charges against the accused, the integrity of the justice system, and the nature and gravity of the violation of Mr. Bellusci’s rights. Only then did he conclude that a stay was warranted.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge balanced competing interests and then concluded a stay was warranted.

propositions.text: Appellate courts must defer to trial judges’ broad discretion under s. 24(1) of the Charter absent legal or factual error.
propositions.quote: But absent an error of law or reviewable finding of fact, appellate courts must defer to the broad discretion vested in trial judges by s. 24(1) of the Charter .

propositions.text: Appellate courts must not substitute their discretion for trial judges’ merely because they would have granted a different remedy.
propositions.quote: appellate courts must take particular care not to substitute their own exercise of discretion for that of the trial judge merely because they would have granted a more generous or more limited remedy” (para. 42).

paragraphs.summary: The Court states appellate courts must defer to trial judges’ discretion under s. 24(1) and not substitute their own remedy preferences.

propositions.text: The trial judge carefully considered relevant principles, assessed prejudice gravity, and explained why alternatives were inadequate.
propositions.quote: In short, the trial judge in this case carefully and correctly considered all the relevant principles. He assessed the gravity of the prejudice and explained why he thought alternative remedies were inadequate.

propositions.text: The trial judge did not misdirect on law or commit reviewable factual error in granting stay.
propositions.quote: He did not misdirect himself on the applicable law or commit a reviewable error of fact.

propositions.text: The trial judge’s discretion to grant stay was not clearly wrong or an injustice.
propositions.quote: Nor was his exercise of discretion to grant a stay of proceedings “so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice” (Regan, supra).

propositions.text: Other judges have found stay of proceedings proportionate for law enforcement mistreatment.
propositions.quote: other judges have considered a stay of proceedings to be a proportionate remedy for mistreatment suffered at the hands of law enforcement officers: R. v. Walcott (2008), 57 C.R. (6th) 223 (Ont. S.C.J.); R. v. Maskell, 2011 ABPC 176, 512 A.R. 372; R. v. Jackson, 2011 ONCJ 228, 235 C.R.R. (2d) 289; R. v. Mohmedi, 2009 ONCJ 533, 72 C.R. (6th) 345; R. v. J.W., 2006 ABPC 216, 398 A.R. 374; R. v. R.L.F., 2005 ABPC 28, 373 A.R. 114; R. v. Wiscombe, 2003 BCPC 418 (CanLII); R. v. Murphy (2001), 29 M.V.R. (4th) 50 (Sask. Prov. Ct.); R. v. Spannier, 1996 CanLII 978 (B.C.S.C.).

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the trial judge properly exercised discretion to grant stay, supported by precedent for law enforcement mistreatment.

propositions.text: Appellate intervention to overturn the stay was unwarranted.
propositions.quote: With respect, appellate intervention in these circumstances was therefore unwarranted.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds appellate intervention unwarranted.

propositions.text: Whether a court of appeal may remit a matter to trial court for continuation after setting aside a stay of proceedings.
propositions.quote: I turn now to consider whether a court of appeal, upon setting aside a stay of proceedings, may in appropriate circumstances remit the matter to the trial court for continuation of the trial.

paragraphs.summary: The Court raises the issue whether an appellate court can remit a matter to trial court after setting aside a stay.

propositions.text: Section 686(4)(b) allows court of appeal to order new trial, enter guilty verdict, or remit matter to trial court after allowing Crown appeal against acquittal.
propositions.quote: Section 686(4) (b) provides that a court of appeal, upon allowing an appeal by the Crown against an acquittal at trial, may (i) order a new trial, or (ii) except where the verdict is that of a court composed of a judge and jury, enter a verdict of guilty with respect to the offence of which, in its opinion, the accused should have been found guilty but for the error in law, and pass a sentence that is warranted in law, or remit the matter to the trial court and direct the trial court to impose a sentence that is warranted in law.

propositions.text: Acquittal includes stay of proceedings as it ends proceedings favorably to accused (R. v. Jewitt).
propositions.quote: It is well established that “acquittal”, in this context, includes a stay of proceedings, since it brings the proceedings to a final conclusion in favour of the accused: R. v. Jewitt, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 128.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains s. 686(4)(b) powers and that acquittal includes stay of proceedings.

propositions.text: Section 686(8) allows court of appeal to make any additional order that justice requires when exercising powers under s. 686(4).
propositions.quote: Section 686(8) provides, in turn, that a court of appeal, upon exercising any of its powers under s. 686(4) , “may make any order, in addition, that justice requires”.

paragraphs.summary: Section 686(8) authorizes additional orders that justice requires when exercising s. 686(4) powers.

propositions.text: It is thought s. 686(8) orders can only be made if court substitutes conviction or orders new trial under s. 686(4).
propositions.quote: Understandably, the phrase “in addition” has been thought to connote that a court of appeal, in setting aside an acquittal or stay of proceedings, may make an order under s. 686(8) only if it substitutes a conviction or orders a new trial ― its only powers explicitly conferred by s. 686(4) .

paragraphs.summary: It is argued s. 686(8) orders require substitution of conviction or new trial under s. 686(4).

propositions.text: R. v. Hinse holds s. 686(8) must be liberally interpreted for broad remedial purpose, allowing orders even without prior s. 686 powers exercised.
propositions.quote: in R. v. Hinse, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 597, Lamer C.J. held that s. 686(8) must be given a large and liberal interpretation consistent with its “broad remedial purpose” (para. 30; see also R. v. Provo, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 3, at p. 20). And, although the Chief Justice considered that s. 686(8) orders are “fundamentally ancillary and supplemental” (para. 31), he nonetheless held that “a court of appeal may enter an order under its residual power even if the court of appeal has not previously and independently ‘exercise[d] any of the powers conferred by subsection (2), (4), (6) or (7)’ of s. 686” (para. 30). This solution was adopted by the Alberta Court of Appeal in R. v. Yelle, 2006 ABCA 276, 397 A.R. 287.

paragraphs.summary: R. v. Hinse holds s. 686(8) must be liberally interpreted to allow orders even without prior s. 686 powers exercised.

propositions.text: R. v. Smith confirms s. 686(8) applies broadly to any power exercised under s. 686(2), allowing additional orders.
propositions.quote: In R. v. Smith, 2004 SCC 14, [2004] 1 S.C.R. 385, Binnie J. reached the same conclusion by a route that conforms more closely to the text of s. 686(8) .

propositions.text: Quashing conviction under s. 686(2) is an exercise of power triggering s. 686(8) for additional orders.
propositions.quote: Section 686(2) provides that where a Court of Appeal allows an appeal, “it shall quash the conviction”, and s. 686(8) provides that, on the exercise of “any of the powers” under s. 686(2), the court may make “any order, in addition, that justice requires”. The quashing of the conviction is an exercise of the court’s power under s. 686(2). [para. 22]

paragraphs.summary: R. v. Smith confirms s. 686(8) applies broadly to powers exercised under s. 686(2), allowing additional orders.

propositions.text: The same reasoning applies to s. 686(4); appellate court need not order new trial or guilty verdict to trigger s. 686(8).
propositions.quote: The same reasoning applies to s. 686(4) . In allowing the appeal and setting aside the acquittal (or stay of proceedings), the court exercises a power under s. 686(4) . It follows, in my view, that an appellate court need not order a new trial or enter a verdict of guilty in order to trigger the application of s. 686(8) , which depends only on the exercise of “any of the powers” conferred by s. 686(4) .

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes s. 686(8) applies once s. 686(4) power is exercised, without needing new trial or guilty verdict.

propositions.text: Section 686(8) authorizes appellate court to order trial continuation if justice requires, but order must not contradict underlying judgment.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, s. 686(8), which allows “any order . . . that justice requires”, authorizes an appellate court to order the continuation of a trial ― but only where continuation of the trial is what “justice requires” in the particular circumstances of the case. Manifestly, an order under s. 686(8) must not be at variance with the underlying judgment: R. v. Thomas, [1998] 3 S.C.R. 535, at para. 17.

paragraphs.summary: Section 686(8) allows appellate court to order trial continuation if justice requires, consistent with underlying judgment.

propositions.text: Alberta Court of Appeal set aside stay but declined conviction or new trial, ordered trial continuation as justice required
propositions.quote: the Alberta Court of Appeal set aside a stay of proceedings, but declined to either substitute a conviction or order a new trial. Instead, the court ordered continuation of the trial because that is what justice required in the circumstances of the case

propositions.text: Ordering new trial would require rehearing three months of evidence for no good reason
propositions.quote: The implications of ordering a new trial would be enormous in a case such as this. It would require the rehearing of three months of evidence for no good reason

propositions.text: New trial unnecessary, wasteful of court resources, witnesses' time, and respondents' money
propositions.quote: In addition to being completely unnecessary, it would be a great waste of the court’s resources, the witnesses’ time, and the respondents’ money (requiring them to pay again for legal services already provided)

propositions.text: No advantage to parties or justice administration to start anew; prejudice to parties, witnesses, and justice reputation
propositions.quote: there is no advantage to the parties or the administration of justice to start anew. Indeed, there will be prejudice to all involved; the parties, witnesses, and the reputation of the administration of justice

paragraphs.summary: The Alberta Court of Appeal set aside the stay but ordered trial continuation, finding a new trial unnecessary and prejudicial to all involved.

propositions.text: Trial continuation is not always preferable or possible; it requires justice, no undue prejudice, and no unfairness
propositions.quote: Continuation of the trial will not always be preferable or even possible. It is in any event an order that can properly be made only where the interests of justice require it, where there is no undue prejudice to the parties, and where no unfairness would result

paragraphs.summary: The court states trial continuation requires justice, no undue prejudice, and no unfairness, and is not always preferable or possible.

propositions.text: Trial court retains discretion to order new trial if resumption is impractical or unfair
propositions.quote: the trial court to which the matter is remitted should retain its discretion to instead order a new trial where resumption of the interrupted proceedings proves to be impractical or unfair

paragraphs.summary: The court holds the trial court should retain discretion to order a new trial if resumption is impractical or unfair.

propositions.text: Both parties agree court of appeal may order trial continuation after setting aside stay
propositions.quote: both parties agree that a court of appeal may order continuation of the trial upon setting aside a stay of proceedings

propositions.text: Both parties submit conviction should be entered if stay overturned, as relevant findings of fact already made
propositions.quote: They both submit, however, that a conviction should instead be entered in this case if the stay is overturned, since the relevant findings of fact have in their view already been made

paragraphs.summary: Both parties agree trial continuation is possible but argue conviction should be entered if stay is overturned.

propositions.text: Stay was wrongly set aside by Court of Appeal; no need to decide on trial resumption order
propositions.quote: I find it unnecessary to express a decided view regarding its order that the trial should be resumed

propositions.text: There appears merit in amicus curiae's submission that conviction was not a foregone conclusion
propositions.quote: there appears to be merit in the submission of the amicus curiae that a conviction was not a foregone conclusion

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the stay was wrongly set aside and sees merit in amicus curiae's view that conviction was not certain.

propositions.text: Indictment alleges physical violence under s. 423.1(1)(b) and (2)(a), but accused found guilty only of verbal threats under different subsection
propositions.quote: the indictment against Mr. Bellusci alleges physical violence, contrary to s. 423.1(1) (b) and (2) (a), whereas Mr. Bellusci was only found to have uttered verbal threats, an offence under a different subsection of the Code

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the indictment alleges physical violence but the accused was found guilty only of verbal threats under a different subsection.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed and stay of proceedings restored
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal and restore the stay of proceedings entered by the trial judge. Appeal allowed and stay of proceedings restored

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal and restores the stay of proceedings entered by the trial judge.
